There is a part hiding inside your microwave oven that was never meant to be understood, only to be obeyed.

Engineers call it a transformer. Scrap dealers call it free money. Anyone who has ever put a meter on the right wire calls it something they can't repeat in public.

Here is the secret: it doesn't matter how many volts it makes. What matters is what happens when you stop asking for volts and start demanding amps.

Because volts are the thing that scare you.

Amps are the thing that melt steel.

This is a long one. Do not skim it. By the last line you will never look at a wall socket, a phone charger, a power line, or a car battery the same way again.

And then you'll scroll back up and watch that video a second time with completely different eyes.

Let's go.

1. THE BIGGEST LIE YOU WERE TOLD ABOUT ELECTRICITY

Somewhere around age eight, someone taught you that voltage is the dangerous one.

Yellow signs. A skull. A lightning bolt. "DANGER: 10,000 VOLTS."

Nobody has ever hung a sign that says "DANGER: 10,000 AMPS." And that is strange, because volts do not do the work.

Volts are pressure. Volts are potential. Volts are a promise.

Amps are delivery.

Volts are the size of the loan. Amps are how much money actually changes hands.

A doorknob spark on a dry winter day can be several thousand volts, sometimes more than ten thousand. It has never destroyed anything but your mood, because almost no charge moves. The promise was huge and the delivery was a rounding error.

Now flip it.

A car battery is a humble 12 volts. Touch both terminals with your fingers and you will feel nothing at all. Lay a steel wrench across them and that wrench can turn red, weld itself to the post, and throw molten droplets across the garage. Same battery. Same 12 volts. Wildly different ending.

Voltage decides whether current can get through something. Current decides what it does to that thing on the way.

Read that twice. Almost every electrical myth you believe dies right there.

2. THE ONE EQUATION THAT RUNS THE PHYSICAL WORLD

If you only remember one line from this entire post, make it this one:

Heat equals current squared, times resistance.

Engineers write it as P = I^2 x R. Say it out loud: I squared R.

Not current times resistance. Current SQUARED.

That little exponent is the most important exponent in electrical engineering, and it is a trap for human intuition, because we think in straight lines and nature does not.

Take a scrap of conductor with a resistance of just one milliohm. One thousandth of an ohm. Basically nothing. A stub of thick wire, a slightly loose clamp, a smudge of oxide on a joint.

At 10 amps it dissipates one tenth of a watt. You can't feel it.

At 100 amps it dissipates 10 watts. Warm to the touch, like a phone left in the sun.

At 1,000 amps it dissipates 1,000 watts. That is a kitchen space heater, concentrated in a spot the size of your thumb.

At 10,000 amps it dissipates 100,000 watts. One hundred kilowatts. The output of a small industrial furnace, crammed into a piece of metal you could hide in a fist.

The resistance never changed. The material never changed. The only thing that changed was the current, and the heat went up not ten times per step, but one hundred times.

Ten times the current. One hundred times the fire.

That is why a wire that carries a hair dryer is boring, and the same wire carrying a thousand times more is a blowtorch with no fuel.

Nothing here needs fuel. Electricity is simply refusing to squeeze through a narrow place quietly.

And if you think that's dramatic, wait until you see how high the numbers actually go.

3. THE AMP LADDER (EVERY RUNG IS WORSE THAN THE LAST)

Let's climb. Hold on to something.

RUNG 1: 0.001 amps (one milliamp)
You can just barely feel it. A faint tingle. Your nervous system files it under "weird."

RUNG 2: 0.01 amps (ten milliamps)
The muscles in your hand can clamp shut around the source. You do not decide to let go. Your arm has stopped taking orders. This is why the scariest thing about small currents is not the pain. It is the loss of a vote.

RUNG 3: 0.1 amps (a tenth of an amp)
Across the chest, for long enough, this is in the range where a heart loses its rhythm. One tenth of one amp. About the current of a small 12 watt bulb. Your entire life is sitting on a margin that thin.

RUNG 4: 15 amps
The breaker in your wall. A kettle, a toaster, a hair dryer all live here. On a 120 volt circuit that is 1,800 watts, enough to boil a liter of water in about three minutes. It is also the ceiling of what your house wiring will tolerate for long before it starts complaining with heat.

RUNG 5: 300 amps
Your car starter motor, cranking a cold engine. Your whole life you have turned a key and asked a small metal cylinder for more current than the main breaker of many homes is even rated to pass. You did it half asleep, holding coffee.

RUNG 6: 10,000 amps
Welcome to the industrial world. Resistance spot welding, the technique that fuses the thin steel panels of a car body, pushes thousands to tens of thousands of amps through a contact patch for a fraction of a second. A modern car carries thousands of those welds. Each one was a tiny, controlled, deliberate lightning strike.

RUNG 7: 11,850 amps
The nominal current in the superconducting magnets that steer protons around the Large Hadron Collider, held at 1.9 kelvin. That is colder than deep space. Not a coincidence. We will come back to that.

RUNG 8: 30,000 amps
A typical lightning stroke. The strong ones climb past 200,000. The air along the channel briefly reaches roughly 30,000 kelvin, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, and the thunder you hear is the air itself being blown outward faster than the speed of sound.

RUNG 9: 100,000 amps
The electrodes of an electric arc furnace, the machine that recycles scrap steel by lighting an arc between graphite rods as thick as a barrel and the metal itself. The arc runs at temperatures far above the melting point of anything it touches. Steel does not resist. It just becomes a liquid you can pour.

RUNG 10: 500,000 amps
A single cell in a modern aluminum smelter, running around the clock at just four or five volts. Four volts. Less than a laptop charger, at a current that adds up to roughly two megawatts per cell. Rows of these cells form a line up to about a kilometer long, and it never turns off, because switching it off can freeze the metal inside and wreck the whole plant.

RUNG 11: about 1,000,000 amps
The electromagnetic railgun, an experimental weapon that uses a pulse of current on the order of a million amps to accelerate a projectile to several times the speed of sound with no gunpowder at all. The forces involved are so violent that the rails themselves get eroded by the very thing that launches the shell.

RUNG 12: 26,000,000 amps
The Z Machine at Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico. For roughly a hundred billionths of a second, it slams tens of millions of amps into a target the size of a spool of thread. Metal wires do not melt. They turn into plasma and get crushed by their own magnetic field. Researchers there have reported temperatures in the billions of degrees.

Look at the pattern on that ladder.

On the working rungs, volts barely move. A smelter cell runs on less voltage than a laptop charger. A spot welder runs on a handful of volts. A car starter runs on twelve.

The headline number, every single time, is the amps.

That should bother you. It bothers everyone who realizes it. Because the natural next question is:

How do you even make that much current from a wall socket?

Keep reading. The answer is an idea so simple it will feel like cheating.

4. THE ONLY HONEST TRICK IN ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING

Energy cannot be created. Everyone agrees on that. It is the one rule the universe never bends.

But energy can be traded. And the cleanest trade ever invented is two coils of wire wrapped around a lump of iron.

That is a transformer. It has no moving parts. No software. No fuel. It just sits there humming, and it does something that sounds illegal.

It trades pressure for flow.

Power is volts times amps. Put 120 volts and 10 amps into one side and you are feeding it 1,200 watts. A good transformer hands almost all of that back out the other side, but you choose the shape of it.

Step the voltage up by ten, and the current drops by ten.

Step the voltage down by ten, and the current rises by ten.

Step it down by a hundred, and 10 amps becomes, in an ideal world, 1,000 amps.

The rule is stunningly simple. The ratio of the voltages is the ratio of the turns of wire. The ratio of the currents is the exact opposite. That's it. That is the whole law.

A transformer is a gearbox for electricity. Low gear gives you brute force. High gear gives you speed and reach. You never get free power out of it. You only get to decide what kind of power you receive.

And here is the part almost nobody says out loud:

Big power hides in small voltages just as easily as it hides in big ones. It is the same watts wearing a different outfit.

The appliance that heats your lunch has to make thousands of volts, because that is what its tube demands. But the iron inside it does not care which direction you shift the gears. It was built to climb. Ask it to descend, and the same slab that produced a whisper of current at four figures of volts will hand you a shout of current at almost no volts at all.

That is the loophole. That is why a scrap part from a dumpster is, physically, a cousin of the machines on the ladder above.

Which brings us to the strangest fact in this whole post.

5. WHY ONE VOLT CAN BE MORE DANGEROUS THAN A THOUSAND

You cannot shock yourself on a couple of volts. Your skin's resistance is far too high. The pressure isn't there to push a meaningful current through you.

So the low-voltage, high-current world feels safe in the way a sleeping dog feels safe.

It is not a shock hazard. It is a heat hazard. And heat is indifferent to whether you feel a tingle.

Every mechanic, jeweler, and electrician has heard the same warning: take off your ring. A metal ring that bridges a battery or a heavy bus bar can heat up in seconds. There are real injuries, some terrible, from people who touched a "harmless" 12 volts with one careless piece of jewelry.

Your senses were tuned by evolution to fear the tall thing, the loud thing, the thing that crackles. The quiet thing that just makes metal glow slipped through the filter.

This is why the most respected experts in this world never eyeball anything. They measure. They measure current. They measure temperature. They measure everything, because their instincts have taught them that instinct is exactly the wrong tool here.

The louder the display, the more important it is to remember what you are actually looking at.

6. HEAT LIVES WHERE RESISTANCE LIVES

Here is a riddle that gets more interesting the longer you stare at it.

An incandescent light bulb is plugged into the wall by a cord. The exact same current flows through the cord and through the filament. The cord stays cool. The filament reaches roughly 2,700 degrees Celsius.

Same current. Wildly different outcomes.

The difference is resistance. The current is the same everywhere in a simple loop, but the heat is made only where the path is narrow, thin, dirty, or loose.

So the rule is:

Current is the force. Resistance is the location.

Put a thousand amps through a fat copper bar and nothing much happens. Put the same thousand amps through a spot where two pieces of metal barely touch, and that tiny contact patch turns into the hottest place in the room.

This is not only how welders work. It is how electrical fires start in houses. A slightly loose screw on a terminal. A corroded contact. A plug that isn't fully seated. Nothing dramatic. Just a little extra resistance, doing its I squared R in the dark, for months.

It is why the modern fast chargers for electric cars use heavy cables with liquid coolant running through them. Push several hundred amps through a plug for twenty minutes and copper needs to be cooled or it will cook itself. The newest megawatt chargers for electric trucks target currents up to about 3,000 amps.

Every high-current engineer has the same obsession: find the narrowest point in the loop, because that is where the energy will go to die.

Hold that thought. It applies to more than wires.

7. THE WAR THAT WAS DECIDED BY AN EXPONENT

In the 1880s, the world argued about how to deliver electricity to cities. One camp backed direct current. The other backed alternating current. The public version of the story is a feud between famous men.

The real version is a spreadsheet.

Wires waste energy as heat. That waste is I squared R. To send power a long way, you have two options: use fat, expensive wires, or cut the current.

You cut the current by raising the voltage. Send the same power at 100 times the voltage and the current falls to one hundredth. Because loss scales with the square, the waste falls to one ten-thousandth.

One hundred times the voltage. Ten thousand times less loss.

But in the 1880s there was no easy way to change the voltage of direct current. Alternating current had a superpower: the transformer. Hungarian engineers at the Ganz works showed a practical closed-core design in 1885, and William Stanley built one of the first commercial systems in Massachusetts in 1886.

The transformer decided the winner. Not charisma. Not marketing. A lump of iron and two coils.

Today the biggest lines on Earth run at 765,000 volts and beyond, so that a few hundred amps can move a colossal amount of power across a continent. China operates a line at plus and minus 1,100,000 volts that spans more than 3,000 kilometers and moves on the order of 12 gigawatts.

And at the end of that journey, a substation steps the voltage back down, and the current climbs back up, and it flows into your house at a level that will not cook the walls.

The entire electrical grid is one long argument between volts and amps, refereed by transformers.

The same object that keeps a city lit for a century can, in a very different form, produce a current that vaporizes metal.

That is not a contradiction. That is the same law, run in the other direction.

8. WHEN RESISTANCE DISAPPEARS

Now for the wildest twist in the entire story.

If heat is I squared R, then what happens when R goes to zero?

In 1911, the physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury to about 4 kelvin and watched its electrical resistance vanish. Not shrink. Vanish. He had discovered superconductivity.

With no resistance, there is no I squared R. With no I squared R, there is no heat. And with no heat, you can push absurd currents through a wire, forever.

That is the trick behind the magnets in an MRI machine and in the Large Hadron Collider. Currents of hundreds to thousands of amps, with no meaningful loss, in cables cooled to temperatures colder than the void between galaxies.

Physicists have set current flowing in a closed superconducting loop and then watched it for years without measuring any decay. Their calculations put the lifetime of that current at more than 100,000 years.

A current that outlives every civilization that has ever measured it.

So the story of amps is a story with two poles.

At one end, a normal metal, where current meets resistance and turns into fire.

At the other, a superconductor, where current meets nothing and stays alive indefinitely.

Everything else, every wire, every appliance, every motor, every power plant, lives in between, negotiating.

9. YOUR ENTIRE ROOM WAS ELECTROCUTED INTO EXISTENCE

Look around you.

The aluminum in your phone, your window frames, your soda can: made by pushing enormous direct currents through molten salts. Producing a single kilogram takes on the order of 13 to 15 kilowatt-hours. Across the world, aluminum production consumes roughly three percent of all the electricity generated on the planet.

The steel in the nearest building: a large share of it was melted by an arc furnace.

The copper in the walls: refined by electrolysis, one electrode at a time.

The chlorine that keeps water safe to drink: made by passing current through brine.

Modern civilization is not only powered by electricity. It is manufactured by it.

And the entire stack rests on one number nobody puts on a warning sign.

Not volts.

Amps.

And here is a number to make it land.

An average lightning stroke carries around 30,000 amps and lasts a few millionths of a second. One cell in an aluminum smelter carries roughly sixteen times that, quietly, without a pause, for years. The sky does it once and makes headlines. A factory does it every second of every day and nobody notices.

The most extreme currents on Earth are not in storms. They are in buildings you drive past on the highway.

10. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU KEEP PUSHING

There is a phenomenon so old that people discovered it before they understood it.

In 1774, the English experimenter Edward Nairne discharged a battery of Leyden jars through a thin wire and watched the wire vanish. Not glow. Not soften. Vanish, in a flash of light and a small bang.

Physicists now call it the electrical explosion of wire. It happens when current rises so fast and so high that the metal heats past melting, past boiling, and turns into plasma before it can even move.

There are three regimes, and they map neatly onto how nature responds when you turn up the current:

Low current: the metal warms. Nothing interesting happens.

High current: the metal glows. It softens. It fails at its weakest point.

Extreme current: the metal doesn't fail. It stops being metal.

That last line is the thing to sit with. Materials are not fixed. Steel isn't steel, copper isn't copper. They are what they are at a given energy density, and above that threshold they turn into something else entirely.

Every material has a current at which it stops being itself.

Which raises a question that has nothing to do with electricity.

What is yours?

11. THE PART WHERE I TELL YOU NOT TO BE AN IDIOT

Everything above is physics. It is beautiful, and it is true. It is also the reason this subject has a body count.

The people who work with this kind of energy for a living do not look like daredevils. They look like accountants. They wear the right gear. They lock out the power. They measure twice, then measure again. They treat the boring checklist as the actual product.

Mains-powered iron and copper does not give second chances. Neither do the capacitors that sometimes sit next to it, holding charge long after the plug is pulled. The difference between a pro and a casualty is almost never courage. It is procedure.

If a clip of someone casually doing something outrageous with electricity makes you think "I could do that," the correct reaction is to go and learn the physics first. Study I squared R. Study insulation. Study what a fuse actually protects. Learn the difference between the thing that looks scary and the thing that is scary.

Watch it. Learn from it. Respect it. Do not copy it.

The person who makes it look easy has usually spent years making it boring.

12. THE RULES OF AMPS

Print these. Tape them above your desk.

1. Volts are the promise. Amps are the delivery.

2. Heat is current squared, times resistance. Never forget the square.

3. Double the current and you quadruple the heat. Ten times the current, a hundred times the heat.

4. Current is decided by the load, not by the source. A source only says what it can offer. The circuit decides what it takes.

5. A transformer does not create power. It trades voltage for current, and current for voltage.

6. Lower the voltage by a factor, and the available current rises by the same factor.

7. Low voltage is not the same as low danger. It just moves the danger from your nerves to your skin and your jewelry.

8. Heat concentrates where the path is narrowest, dirtiest, or loosest.

9. The fastest way to start a fire is a connection that is almost good enough.

10. The grid runs on high voltage so that the wires can stay cool.

11. Resistance is the enemy of efficiency and the friend of every heater ever built.

12. Superconductors are what happens when you cheat resistance and pay in cold.

13. Every material has a current where it stops behaving like itself.

14. Never trust your instincts around energy. Trust your meter.

15. If the number on the display frightens you, that is not a bug. It is the point of the display.

13. WHY YOU CANNOT LOOK AWAY

There is a reason a clip like the one above stops your thumb mid-scroll.

Human beings are wired to notice hidden forces becoming visible. Wind you can only see when it bends a tree. Gravity you can only see when something falls. Electricity you can never see at all, until the moment it makes metal do something metal was not supposed to do.

Nothing in your evolutionary history prepared you for a force that is completely silent right up until it isn't. So when it finally shows itself, your brain treats it like a magic trick, and refuses to let go until it understands the trick.

That is the pull. It is the same pull that drew Nairne to his Leyden jars, Kamerlingh Onnes to his cold mercury, and every engineer who ever leaned closer to a scope and said "wait, what?"

Curiosity is not a distraction from serious work. It is where serious work starts.

This is also why the best explanations never begin with the equation. They begin with the moment your jaw drops. The equation is what you reach for afterwards, once you are desperate to know why it happened at all.
And now you know enough to be dangerous in the only good sense of the word: dangerous to your own ignorance.

14. THE MOST DANGEROUS THING IN YOUR KITCHEN IS BORING

Think about how strange this all is.

You own a box that is, by any reasonable definition, an industrial energy device. It sits next to the bread. It has a pretty digital clock. A child can operate it.

Inside is a lump of iron and copper that is physically a relative of the machines that melt scrap steel and smelt the metal in your phone. The only thing separating the two is how it is wired and how hard it is asked to work.

That is the deepest lesson of amps. The world is full of ordinary objects holding extraordinary potential, and what decides which one you get is not the object.

It is the circuit you build around it.

15. WHAT TO CARRY OUT OF HERE

If this post melted your brain a little, here is the compressed version:

Volts push. Amps do.
Heat scales with the square of the current.
Transformers trade pressure for flow.
Low voltage does not mean low danger.
Energy lands where the path is narrowest.
The number on the meter never lies. Only your instincts do.
Every material has a breaking current.
And the most powerful things are usually the quietest ones, right up until they are not.

16. NOW GO BACK TO THE TOP

Scroll up. Press play again.

Sound on.

The first time, you watched a spectacle.

This time, you know about I squared R, about the gearbox made of iron, about the narrowest point in the loop and the number that decides where all that energy has to go.

Do not watch the light. Watch the place it comes from.

You will see what most of the internet will never see: not a stunt, but a law of physics doing exactly what it always does, at a scale your intuition was never built for.

Then tell me in the replies:

What is the largest current you have ever seen on a meter? What surprised you? And what number in your own life have you been ignoring because it is quiet?

If this post taught you one thing you did not know an hour ago, repost it. Somebody in your feed is about to say "it's only twelve volts," and they deserve to hear the rest.

Follow for more posts where a boring object turns out to be a monster in disguise.

Volts get the warning signs.

Amps get the last word.

DEEP-VALUE LEN5, FIVE TO WATCH: INTUITIVE SURGICAL $ISRG HAS ERASED ITS JULY SLIDE. THE PROOF ARRIVES IN OCTOBER:

Intuitive Surgical ISRG at $414.79, +$9.61 / +2.37% on Monday, closed at its highest price since July 8 - above the $402.33 it closed at on July 16, the afternoon it reported a strong quarter and the day before its stock fell 14%. Of the five names the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 is watching here, it is the only one whose price has stopped waiting for evidence.

The other four show what this Len5 is finding right now, and it is not wreckage. All five lead their fields - surgical robots, salvage car auctions, U.S. banking, payroll, and the software community banks run on - and each has been marked down on one specific fear. On each company's latest full year or quarter, four earn more per share than a year earlier; the fifth, Copart, earns 2.5% less. Their stocks sit 8% to 41% under their highs of the past year. So far the prices have moved much further than the profits.

Intuitive makes the da Vinci surgical robot and the instruments surgeons use in each operation on it; 85% of its sales repeat - instruments, service and leases - rather than coming from one-time machine sales. This Len5 picked it as a debt-free leader that an event knocked down harder than the business deserved: $8.6B of cash and investments, no debt, and a stock that fell about 45% from its $603.88 peak on January 7 to $328.57 on July 23.

The July 16 report, quarter to June 30:
- Revenue $2.89B, +19%
- Procedures +16%; U.S. da Vinci +12%, international +20%
- 468 da Vinci systems placed vs 395 a year earlier; 267 in the U.S., +24%
- Profit $2.29 a share vs $1.81, +27%
- First-half free cash flow - cash left after running the business and paying for equipment - $1.76B

What the market sold was the outlook. Intuitive held its 2026 forecast for da Vinci procedure growth at 13.5% to 15.5% rather than raising it, and named the drags: changes to Affordable Care Act premium subsidies that may be leading some patients to put off surgery, bariatric operations down high single digits as weight-loss drugs spread, and a tougher China. Six days later, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) at $271.95, +$0.73 / +0.27% on Monday, won FDA authorization for Ottava, a surgical robot built into the operating table, cleared for ten general-surgery procedures from gallbladder removal to gastric bypass and launching with select U.S. hospitals. J&J sits on this same Len5, for a drug-and-device franchise whose value holds up even after counting all of its debt.

Intuitive is up 24.9% from its July 23 close of $332.02. Monday's gain came as the 10-year Treasury yield - what the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years - closed at 5.24%, up 0.06 point, the kind of day that usually hits richly priced stocks hardest. The strongest fact against it is that price: about 46 times its last year of profit, with much of the July discount already spent.

J&J reports October 13, its first quarterly report since Ottava was cleared. Intuitive reports October 20 after the close; analysts expect $2.54 a share. The number that decides it is U.S. da Vinci procedure growth, 12% last quarter. What would knock Intuitive off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: U.S. procedure growth slowing again while U.S. system placements fall - the sign hospitals are waiting to compare robots, not waiting on insurance. Verdict: the business came through July intact, and the stock has priced that in before the first evidence on the rival arrives.

The Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 hunts a sound business priced below a cautious estimate of what it is worth - or one an event has knocked down harder than the business deserves.

- Copart (CPRT) at $27.22, -$0.37 / -1.34% on Monday. It runs online auctions for wrecked and totaled cars, mostly for insurers. The Len5 picked it for its yard network, hard to copy because few places will zone land for acres of wrecked cars. Its special situation lands tomorrow: Copart's $10.50-a-share cash offer for ACV Auctions (ACVA) at $10.46, +$0.00 / +0.00% on Monday, an online dealer-to-dealer used-car marketplace, expires one minute after 11:59pm ET Wednesday unless extended, and needs a majority of ACV's shares tendered plus U.S. antitrust clearance. ACV is on none of the six Len5 watchlists; its price simply tracks the offer. September 10, year to July 31: profit $1.55 a share, -2.5%; $4.5B of cash and securities, no debt; $1.6B of buybacks. U.S. insurance volume fell 7.5% in the quarter, but would have risen 2.3% without one insurer it lost. About 18 times profit, 41% under its October 2025 high of $45.89. What would knock Copart off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: U.S. insurance volume falling even with that lost customer set aside, in the report tentatively due November 19. Verdict: priced like a shrinking business after losing one account.

- JPMorgan Chase (JPM) at $336.59, -$6.47 / -1.89% on Monday. The largest U.S. bank: checking accounts, credit cards, business loans, dealmaking and trading. The Len5 picked it as a top-quality lender valued on its earnings with one-time gains taken out. On that basis, July 14: $6.14 a share, leaving out $1.56 a share of one-time investment gains, vs $4.96 a year earlier, +24%; net interest income - what it earns on loans minus what it pays depositors - $25.6B, +10%; trading revenue $12.1B, +35%; dealmaking fees $3.3B, +30%. It paid $4.0B of dividends and bought back $6.2B of stock in the quarter, and the dividend rises to $1.65 from $1.50 for holders of record October 6. The stock fell 3.4% on September 22, a day 24/7 Wall St. tied bank selling to the 10-year near 5% and a nearly flat yield curve - little gap between short- and long-term rates, which squeezes what a bank earns borrowing short and lending long. It fell another 1.9% Monday. About 15 times its cleaned-up profit, 8% under its August 13 high. What would knock JPMorgan off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: trading and dealmaking falling back hard on October 13, proof the $6.14 was a peak rather than a base; analysts expect $5.88. Verdict: a bank earning 24% more per share than a year ago, marked down for the rate climate around it.

- Automatic Data Processing (ADP) at $261.80, -$1.87 / -0.71% on Monday. It runs payroll and HR for businesses from one-person shops to multinationals. The Len5 picked it as the dominant payroll processor, valued even after charging for its software spending and the stock it pays employees. July 29, fiscal year to June: revenue $21.9B, +7%; adjusted profit - leaving out one-time items - $11.12 a share, +11%; $4.7B returned in dividends and buybacks. Higher rates quietly help: ADP holds client payroll money before paying it out - $40.4B on average last year, earning 3.4% - and expects about 3.7% this year, lifting that interest income to $1.54B-$1.56B from $1.36B. The fear is hiring: pays per control, the number of workers on each U.S. client's payroll, grew 1% last year and is planned at 0% to 1%. About 24 times profit, 11% under the $294.35 high it set a year ago today. What would knock ADP off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: pays per control shrinking in the October 28 report, where analysts expect $2.77 a share. Verdict: a steady compounder with one line, client interest, that the rate climb is paying for.

- Jack Henry & Associates (JKHY) at $147.82, +$0.03 / +0.02% on Monday. The Missouri company runs the core systems - deposits, loans, the ledger - for community banks and credit unions, and moving off one takes a bank years. The Len5 picked it as a sticky franchise priced below what its current earnings support. August 18, fiscal year to June: revenue $2.54B, +7%; profit $6.98 a share, +12%; a record 58 banks and credit unions won from rivals, 14 of them with more than $1B of assets. The soft spot is the last quarter: $1.57 a share vs $1.75 a year earlier, -10%, on higher staff and research spending. It bought back $448M of stock in the year at an average $152, above today's price. Its plan for fiscal 2027 is $7.33-$7.38 a share - about 20 times at today's price, 24% under its January high of $193.39. What would knock Jack Henry off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: a second straight quarter of shrinking profit in the report tentatively due November 3. Verdict: a record year of client wins, priced as if the soft quarter were the trend.

Four of these five still carry their fear in the price. Intuitive has already set its fear down, three weeks before hospitals give their first real answer on the rival robot - which makes it the one name here where the stock, not the company, has something to prove.

Not investment advice.

Elon Musk is criticizing New York’s voting rules after his mother, Maye Musk, said a woman at a polling place angrily knocked away the ID she offered while voting.

Maye Musk, the 78-year-old model, dietitian, and author, was responding to a list of the 14 states that still refuse to require voter ID at the polls. Those states, as conservatives have noted for years, reliably deliver Democratic wins.

“Definitely New York,” she wrote. “When I voted and showed my ID, the woman was angry and hit it away.”

Definitely New York. When I voted and showed my ID, the woman was angry and hit it away. https://t.co/NXK0Op7iMC— Maye Musk (@mayemusk) September 27, 2026

That is not a first for Maye. During the 2024 cycle she said early voting in New York City required no ID at all and that workers “won’t even look at your ID.” Later she described being told to sign a form, stuff it in an envelope, and drop it in a box while the worker “refused to see my ID.”

After his mother, Maye Musk, described being met with hostility when she tried to show identification at a New York polling place, the X owner dropped a charge that Democrats in the country’s two largest blue states have spent years pretending is “disinformation.”

In New York and California, they have made it illegal for officials to ask for or for you to show your voter ID!They made election fraud mandatory. https://t.co/mxvjfv7DDq— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) September 27, 2026

Don’t take Musk’s word for it. Take Letitia James.

The New York Attorney General’s official voting-resources page states, in black and white, that voters “are never required to present photo identification to cast an in-person ballot” and instructs New Yorkers: “If you see or hear of anyone improperly requesting voter identification, contact OAG.” Read it here.

Poll-worker guidance tracks the same line: do not ask for ID unless the voter file is already flagged. Signature matching is the substitute. No photo. No citizenship check at the table. Just a scribble.

That is why a poll worker would get angry at a woman holding out a government ID. The training says don’t look. The AG’s office says report the person who asks.

California is even more aggressive. In 2024, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 1174, which bars cities and counties from requiring identification at the polls, a direct strike at Huntington Beach after voters there passed their own ID rule. Courts later killed the local measure. Sacramento made sure no charter city could close the barn door.

As The Gateway Pundit reported last month, California still lets applicants register online with no driver’s license and no Social Security number. The state’s own acceptable-ID list for the rare first-time voter who actually gets asked includes a gym card, an insurance card, or a credit card.

You can vote for governor with a Planet Fitness membership. You cannot cash a paycheck with one.

The hypocrisy is not subtle.

According to Fox News, New York City demanded two photos, two original IDs, and a Social Security card from emergency snow shovelers last winter, the same city that tells election inspectors not to look at a voter’s license.

As The Gateway Pundit reported in August, Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani floated ID requirements for his government grocery stores so people wouldn’t resell discounted food. President Trump’s response was the obvious one: they will check your papers to buy milk, but not to choose the people who run the country.

Need a beer? ID. Board a plane? ID. Pick up a prescription? ID. Decide who controls the House in November? In New York and California, that is treated like a poll tax.

text:
After the release of Step 5 Preview, @StepFun_ai  co-founder Yibo Zhu took a closer look at an idea the team has been exploring over the past few months: can training also benefit from “PD separation”?

He shared his answer on Zhihu: KV-Invariant Transformer Expansion for Efficient Agentic LLM Scaling—a firsthand technical deep dive into a potential new path for scaling agentic LLMs.

🔗 https://t.co/bkqAUul3yr

The core challenge is optimizing three things at once: model quality, training cost, and inference cost.

MoE is a classic example of this “three-way win.” But approaches such as Upcycling and YOCO often trade off one dimension against another: scaling them to recover model quality can increase training or inference costs.

KITE combines scaling with upcycling, while keeping KV computation invariant.

First, a smaller prefiller is trained to generate the KV cache. The model is then expanded with decoder-side components that reuse this KV and continue pretraining. Because these added components do not affect KV computation, the model can scale up to recover quality without proportionally increasing prefill cost.

This is particularly relevant in the Agent era, where long-context workloads can make prefill a major part of inference cost.

Using a simple Step Scale Transformer (SST), the paper demonstrates a three-way gain over a proportionally scaled classical Transformer baseline: better model quality, lower training cost, and lower inference cost.

KITE is ultimately a broader principle of KV-invariant scaling, rather than a single architecture. Better prefiller/decoder designs, KV usage strategies, and scaling laws remain open questions.

If agentic workloads continue to be prefill-heavy, KITE could offer an interesting path toward more efficient LLM scaling.

KITE has not yet been applied to Step 5, but similar ideas may eventually appear in StepFun’s mainline models.
